title: The Priesthood and Covenant
summary: Part 5 opens with Jesus’ baptism as the hinge between the Levitical priesthood and the new priesthood after the order of Melchizedek, a priesthood the series says now includes every human being. The duty of this priesthood is to apply Christ’s finished work to creation, and because the priest’s verdict stands (John 20:23), believers must give up accusation or they will hold creation in bondage. Using Joshua and the crossing of the Jordan, the preacher argues that grace brings people out of bondage, but entering the promise takes a whole community acting in maturity, and forerunners have to show mercy to those who are not there yet. Stephen, who forgave his killers, is set against Peter’s handling of Ananias and Sapphira. That contrast leads into a three-heavens model of spirit, soul and body, and a teaching that transfiguration (metamorphoō) through the renewed mind is how the sons of God are revealed. The part closes in 2 Cor 3, read as a contrast between only two glories: the law’s glory of death and the Spirit’s glory of life.
thesis: Believers are a Melchizedek priesthood whose forgiveness or accusation decides whether creation is freed, and by choosing to forgive with renewed minds they are transfigured so that divine life shows in their bodies.

flow.text: Jesus’ baptism by John is presented as the moment the Levitical priesthood handed over to a new priest of Judah’s line, ordained in the order of Melchizedek.
The new priesthood is not tied to a family. All humanity is brought into it, and its task is to apply Christ’s finished work to creation.

flow.step: The verdict of the priest stands
flow.text: John 20:23 shows that the sins believers forgive are forgiven and the sins they retain are retained, so holding creation in accusation kills it.

Churches are described in three levels: body-focused legalism, soul-focused charismatic life, and the 100-fold church of all humanity. Only giving up accusation lets the 100-fold church inspire the others rather than empty them.
God gave the land to Joshua, and Israel received it through him. In the same way Christ, the revealed head, has won a victory the body must take hold of together.
At the Red Sea God did everything. At the Jordan Israel had to be circumcised and step into the water first, which shows that entering the promise takes a deliberate act of will.
Joshua and Caleb went back into the wilderness with the people instead of going in alone. Forerunners today must act as merciful priests for those who are not yet ready.
Peter retained the sins of Ananias and Sapphira and they died. Stephen forgave his murderers, saw Jesus standing, and opened the way for Saul’s conversion.

flow.step: Three heavens, three parts of a person
flow.text: Spirit (third heaven), soul (second heaven) and body (first heaven) each occupy a realm. Believers govern from the spirit instead of fighting in the second heaven.

flow.step: Body and the manifestation of sons
flow.text: Dominion on earth comes through a body, so losing the body means losing one’s destiny. The sons are revealed when what God says about them matches what creation experiences.
Jesus’ transfiguration showed His divinity in His body and gave Him dominion over death. Romans 12:2 uses the same word for what renewing the mind does to believers.
Renewal does not mean fixing the old mind. The carnal mind has died, and believers now hold Christ’s own mind (1 Cor 2:16).
Moses’ face shone with the law’s glory of death and condemnation. Believers looking at the Lord are transfigured from that glory into the glory of the Spirit.
The folded head-cloth shows the head unveiled. The victory Christ has is given to His body, and forgiving persecutors is the way into that same image.

teachings.title: John the Baptist and Jesus’ timing
teachings.body: John was the son of Zechariah and Elizabeth and six months older than Jesus. The preacher says Jesus submitted to the temple’s rules and waited until thirty to begin ministry, which he gives as the age for being a rabbi.

teachings.title: John’s baptism as a ‘Messiah test’
teachings.body: The series rejects the idea that Jesus was baptized because good Jews were baptized, and says Jews did not practise baptism. In the preacher’s account, John’s baptism was a search for the Messiah: John had been told the one on whom the dove landed was the One, so he immersed people until the sign came. This shows how ordinary Jesus’ humanity looked.

teachings.title: Baptism as priestly ordination
teachings.body: Jesus asked John to baptize Him to fulfil all righteousness. The preacher reads this as John, a Levite, performing the Levitical cleansing of a new priest on a man from Judah. In doing so the old priesthood humbly handed everything over. John’s ‘I must decrease’ shows how humble it was to pass his ministry to Jesus after only a short time.

teachings.title: Foreshadowed at the Jordan in Joshua
teachings.body: When Israel saw the priests with the ark standing in the Jordan, it was time to cross. The preacher treats this as a prophetic picture of the priestly transition at Jesus’ baptism in the same river.

teachings.title: From the Levitical to the Melchizedek priesthood
teachings.body: The old priests served at the old covenant altar and offered sacrifices for people under the law. The Melchizedek priesthood has no priestly family, because every human being is brought into it. So believers are not only bride, sons and one with God. They are also a royal priesthood with a responsibility.

teachings.title: The priest’s task: applying the finished work to creation
teachings.body: If humanity is responsible for the redemption of creation, then a priest’s verdict about creation stands. When Jesus sent the disciples as the Father had sent Him, He tied it to forgiving and retaining sins. The preacher concludes that holding creation in accusation kills it.

teachings.title: Judging by natural and by ‘spiritual’ things
teachings.body: Some denominations judge people by outward things such as dress, music and gender. Charismatic churches often judge in a more spiritual-sounding way, through ‘prayer requests’ that are really gossip. Both block the new-creation community from leading the wider body into freedom.

teachings.title: Three levels of church: 30-, 60-, 100-fold
teachings.body: Borrowing a fellow teacher’s terms, the preacher describes the 30-fold church as natural and body-focused. It wants a rapture and to escape. The 60-fold church is focused on spiritual gifts, lives on earth from heaven’s supply, wants revival, and can be elitist toward the first. The 100-fold church wants to reign, but it cannot reign alone, because the promise has to be applied to the whole body.

teachings.title: The 100-fold church includes all humanity
teachings.body: Everyone is a member of the 100-fold church, but only those who know they are members can see the other members. Hebrews 12 describes coming to Mount Zion, the heavenly city, the angels and the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and the preacher takes it to mean the whole of humanity is there. The new-creation church will either inspire every other church or empty it, depending on whether it gives up accusation.

teachings.title: ‘Thank God I’m not like them’ is the mark of the unjustified
teachings.body: In the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, the man who thanked God he was not like others went home unjustified. So agreement, denominational lines, philosophies and theologies must no longer decide whom believers see and how they see them.

teachings.title: Creation waits on the manifested sons
teachings.body: The redemption of creation depends entirely on the sons of God being revealed. If new-creation believers stay in small separate groups, they cannot enter the promise alone.

teachings.title: A vicarious victor in Joshua
teachings.body: God told Joshua that every place his foot trod had been given to him, and then said the land was being given to the people. The preacher reads this as one man’s finished victory being applied to and expressed through a whole community, a picture of Christ and His body.

teachings.title: No entering alone
teachings.body: Joshua and Caleb were ready to go in, but the bad report of the other spies turned the nation back. The preacher puts God’s word as: go back, become one mind and one accord, try again. He suggests the way to transform the body may be forgiveness rather than education.

teachings.title: The head revealed: the folded head-cloth
teachings.body: In John 20 the cloth that had been around Jesus’ head lay folded by itself, apart from the linen wrappings. The preacher calls this a prophetic picture of God’s plan for creation: the head has been revealed, and creation has been given a victory ‘up to the neck’ that the body must now take up.

teachings.title: Hebrews 2: we do not yet see, but we see Jesus
teachings.body: Asked who has ever lived forever, the preacher answers Jesus. Hebrews 2 says God put all creation under humanity’s charge and left nothing outside it. We do not yet see that, but we see Jesus, who has won the victory for us. What He was given He gives to us, as Joshua’s land was given to Israel.

teachings.title: Grace gets you out; maturity gets you in
teachings.body: Entering the promise took a shared conscience and a deliberate act of will. At the Red Sea God told the immature to be still while He fought for them. At the Jordan the answer was ‘your turn’. In the preacher’s paraphrase they were to grow their own food and make their own clothes. Bringing the soul into line with truth is a choice to treat what was won for us as our own portion.

teachings.title: Circumcision at Gilgal: the reproach rolled away
teachings.body: Before entering, the adult men had to be circumcised and rest three days. God said that He had rolled away the reproach of Egypt that day. The preacher reads this as a prophetic act in which everything they were never meant to be was removed before they entered the promise. A related quip: anyone who says you are still under law should be offered an altar call for circumcision.

teachings.title: Stepping into the Jordan
teachings.body: At the Jordan God did not part the water first. The priests had to step in, and then the water stopped and dried up all the way back to a city, which the preacher hints is Adam. He uses this to say that when the soul is consciously aligned with the spirit, everything Adam brought about becomes history.

teachings.title: Forerunners who went back for the people
teachings.body: Instead of entering alone and thinking ‘thank God we’re not like them’, Joshua and Caleb spent forty more years in the wilderness with the people and the next generation. Joshua then made an ‘altar call’ and kept testing the people’s resolve until they truly committed. The whole community then possessed the promise together. Forerunners must show mercy as priests for people who do not yet see themselves as the 100-fold church.

teachings.title: Ananias and Sapphira: sins retained
teachings.body: Ananias and Sapphira were still generous. They sold property and pledged all of it, but lied about the price to look good. Peter said the property and the money had been theirs to use as they wished, with no ten-percent requirement. Their lie shows what religion produces: defeat if you are honest and pride if you lie. Both died. The preacher says Peter, a man with a temper who had already cut off Malchus’ ear, refused to extend forgiveness, and that because of his priestly office their sins were retained.

teachings.title: Against ‘restoring Holy Spirit killings’
teachings.body: The preacher rejects modern claims that God will restore deaths like these to bring back reverence. He asks which is worse for a church, stealing from the offering or murdering its leader. Then he points to Stephen.

teachings.title: Stephen: priesthood in action
teachings.body: Stephen held firm to the revelation of grace and was killed while Saul consented. As he died he asked forgiveness for his killers and saw Jesus standing in heaven. The preacher doubts that Peter saw such a vision when he pronounced sentence on Ananias and Sapphira. Stephen’s plea for his persecutor opened the door to heaven’s help, troubled Saul’s conscience on the road to Damascus, and led to Saul becoming Paul.

teachings.title: Being like your Father is a choice
teachings.body: Matthew teaches that loving and praying for enemies makes you like your Father in heaven. Sometimes resembling the Father is a deliberate act of will.

teachings.title: Conscience shapes the destiny of places
teachings.body: Citing a well-known pastor, the preacher notes that California has the most dangerous weather in the US and is also the state the church judges most. He asks whether a region’s destiny is in the church’s hands. To the pure all things are pure.

teachings.title: Three heavens
teachings.body: Genesis 1:1 speaks of ‘heavens’ in the plural, and Paul speaks of a ‘third heaven’, so there must be a first and a second. The first heaven is what is seen and created, like the body. The second is unseen but created: angels, demons and the soulish realm. The third is ‘heaven in God’, because God does not live in the Kingdom but the Kingdom lives in God.

teachings.title: A person in all three realms
teachings.body: The believer’s spirit is one spirit with the Lord and is unseen and uncreated. The soul occupies the second heaven, and the body, which is distinct from ‘flesh’ as a nature, is the first-heaven point of contact with earth. That makes the body the most important technology in creation. The preacher says God cannot do what a person can do, because only humans were given dominion on earth.

teachings.title: Govern, don’t fight
teachings.body: Spiritual warfare belongs to the second heaven and is not necessary. One born of God does not sin and the evil one cannot touch him. If you are drawn onto the enemy’s ground you play his games, but if you stay in the spirit he has no access. Believers govern rather than fight, and the preacher says this is how transfiguration happens.

teachings.title: Three identities and the role of the body
teachings.body: Third-heaven identity is the Lord from heaven. Second-heaven identity is who the soul believes it is. First-heaven identity is what creation meets in you. Losing the body means losing one’s destiny, which is why the series stresses immortality. Transfiguration is choosing to be governed by the Spirit who gives life to the mortal body. Will belongs to the soul and action to the body. Spirit, soul and body are all to be preserved.

teachings.title: Governance: to will and to do
teachings.body: Christ in you working both to will and to do His good pleasure describes governance. ‘To will’ is the soul’s part and ‘to do’ is the body’s part.

teachings.title: The manifestation of the sons
teachings.body: The sons of God are revealed when what God says about you and what creation experiences in you are the same. A son who is a son only positionally cannot redeem creation, because redemption comes through a physical body. This manifestation is the purpose of the gospel.

teachings.title: Jesus’ transfiguration
teachings.body: On the mountain Jesus’ face shone like the sun and His clothes became white. It was spiritual and also visible: people could see His divinity in His body. The preacher says that from that moment, not from the resurrection, divinity was housed in humanity on earth and Jesus could deal with death as its master rather than its victim. He adds that one does not need to die, or even overcome death, to be divine, because the Spirit gives life to the mortal body, not to death.

teachings.title: Turning the light off and on
teachings.body: Humanity was held in lifelong slavery by fear of death, and the preacher says all fear is rooted in the fear of death. Like a parent who switches the light off and on to show a child there is nothing in the dark, Jesus went into death to show there is nothing to fear.

teachings.title: Romans 12:2: transfigured by renewing the mind
teachings.body: The ‘transformed’ of Romans 12:2 translates metamorphoō, the same verb used of Jesus’ transfiguration. The preacher calls ‘transformed’ a poor translation, because it suggests improving something bad, whereas transfiguration turns humanity into divinity. Renewing the mind is a teaching about governance, and it lets believers prove God’s good, acceptable and perfect will.

teachings.title: We have the mind of Christ
teachings.body: Renewal is not just changing your thoughts. It is realising the carnal mind is gone and dead and that you now have Christ’s mind. Christians sing about God’s ways being mysterious, but 1 Corinthians 2 goes on to say God has revealed these things by His Spirit. To the question of who has known the mind of the Lord, Paul answers that we have the mind of Christ. The preacher reads this as a possessive genitive: Christ’s own mind, not a new mind He made. The goal is to make what has fallen divine, not to fix what is broken.

teachings.title: Stephen’s face like an angel
teachings.body: The word ‘transfigured’ is not used of Stephen, but the preacher sees the thing itself when Stephen chose to be like the Father and people saw a face like an angel’s. The mark of the Father’s heart is blessing those who curse you and praying for those who persecute you. Paul showed it when he was willing to be cut off for the sake of his fellow Jews who persecuted him.

teachings.title: Four uses of metamorphoō
teachings.body: The preacher says the word appears four times in the New Testament: twice of Jesus, once in Romans 12:2 for the renewed mind, and once in 2 Corinthians 3 for believers who behold the Lord.

teachings.title: Doxa and Moses’ shining face
teachings.body: Doxa is defined as ‘the thoughts and opinions of’. It takes its character from whatever it refers to. Moses’ face shone with the glory of the law, which Paul calls the ministry of death and condemnation. So the people avoided him because he was wearing disapproval and death, and he veiled his face because of that covenant, not because of a sight of God.

teachings.title: Jesus shone with the Father’s approval
teachings.body: On the mountain Jesus ‘wore’ the Father’s words: this is My beloved Son, hear Him. His shine drew people from the cities around, because you reflect the God you know. If people run from a believer, it shows which covenant that believer is living in.

teachings.title: The veil removed in Christ
teachings.body: When Moses is read, a veil still lies over the heart, but when someone turns to the Lord it is taken away. The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit is there is freedom. With unveiled faces, beholding the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, believers are transfigured (metamorphoō) into the same image.

teachings.title: Only two glories
teachings.body: The preacher calls it bad doctrine to treat ‘from glory to glory’ as an endless series of spiritual promotions. He says there are only two glories: the glory of death and condemnation, and the glory of Spirit and life. Coming out of the first, believers are transfigured into the Lord’s image.

teachings.title: Government on His shoulders
teachings.body: The prophecy puts the government on the Messiah’s shoulders, not on His head. In other words it rests on His body, while He waits for everything to be put under His feet. The victory given to Him He gives to His people.

teachings.title: Forgiveness is the path into the image
teachings.body: As life-giving spirits, believers must actively forgive their persecutors, and in doing so they are changed into the same image. Stephen’s transfiguration came from choosing to be like his Father. Peter did not glow after Ananias and Sapphira died. Human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.

stories.title: The six-month-old pastor hands over the church
stories.text: The preacher asks the audience to imagine a newly ordained pastor giving the whole church to a newcomer after six months. That is how he pictures John telling his own disciples to follow Jesus. It shows John’s humility and what it cost him with his religious peers.

stories.title: Everyone in line thought they might be Messiah
stories.text: John immersing person after person, effectively saying ‘not you, not you’ until the dove came, is used to show how ordinary Jesus looked. Anyone in that line could have been the One.

stories.title: Gossip dressed up as prayer
stories.text: In charismatic churches, ‘should we pray for them?’ about a rumoured couple is called the cherry on top that makes gossip sound holy. It is an example of spiritual-sounding judgment.

stories.title: Taking people camping who don’t want to go
stories.text: A priest can lead people into freedom against their will. Israel left Egypt kicking and screaming because one mediator decided it was time for them to be free.

stories.title: An altar call for circumcision
stories.text: A Bible teacher known for finding Jesus throughout the Old Testament advised that when someone insists believers are still under the law, you should offer them an altar call for circumcision. The point is that no one really wants the law in full.

stories.title: The altar call that tried to talk people out of it
stories.text: Joshua kept pushing back on Israel’s ‘we will serve the Lord’: you can’t, all your idols must go, the land is held by many hostile kings and giants. He accepted their commitment only when it was sure. The preacher calls it the best altar call ever.

stories.title: Offering theft vs. murdering the pastor
stories.text: The preacher asks which would offend a church more, stealing from the offering or murdering the pastor. Then he sets Ananias and Sapphira, who died for lying about money, beside Stephen, who forgave the men murdering him. Stephen is the model.

stories.title: Saul’s rear-view mirror
stories.text: The preacher imagines Saul on the Damascus road with Stephen’s death behind him, troubled that the man he helped kill begged forgiveness for him. That troubled conscience is part of the context for Saul becoming Paul.

stories.title: California’s weather and the church’s judgment
stories.text: A well-known pastor observed that the state with the most dangerous weather is also the one the church judges most. The preacher uses this to suggest that the church’s conscience affects a region’s destiny.

stories.title: Light off, light on
stories.text: A parent turns the bedroom light off and on to show a frightened child the dark is empty. The preacher says Jesus entered death in the same way to show it holds nothing to fear.

stories.title: The folded head-cloth
stories.text: The head-cloth folded separately in the empty tomb is read as a picture that the head, Christ, has been revealed and has won the victory. The body still has to step into it.

words.claimed: ‘Transfigure’ into a ‘higher form’. The preacher calls ‘transformed’ in Rom 12:2 a bad translation and says the word means turning humanity into divinity, the same as Jesus’ transfiguration.
words.lexicon: BDAG: to change into another form, transform. Used of Jesus’ transfiguration (Matt 17:2; Mark 9:2) and of moral or spiritual change in believers (Rom 12:2; 2 Cor 3:18). The meta- prefix marks change, not a ‘higher’ form. ‘Transformed’ and ‘transfigured’ both translate it correctly. The link between the passages is real, but ‘turning humanity into divinity’ is an interpretation, not part of the word’s meaning.

words.claimed: ‘The thoughts and opinions of’. It has no character of its own and takes on the character of what it refers to, so Moses’ face shone with the law’s ‘opinion’ of disapproval and death.
words.lexicon: In classical Greek doxa does mean opinion, expectation or reputation. In the LXX and the NT it mostly translates Hebrew kabod and means glory, splendour, brightness or honour (BDAG 1–3). In 2 Cor 3:7 it refers to visible radiance. The ‘opinion’ sense does not fit this passage, and the text does not say the radiance was ‘disapproval’.

words.claimed: The plural in Gen 1:1 shows heaven has levels (first, second, third heaven).
words.lexicon: Shamayim always has a plural or dual-looking form in Hebrew, even when it means just the sky, so the form alone does not prove levels. Some Jewish and early Christian writers did teach several heavens (compare 2 Cor 12:2), but the preacher’s specific map (seen and created, unseen and created, heaven in God) is his own theological model.

words.claimed: A possessive genitive: believers have Christ’s own mind, not a mind He made and gave them.
words.lexicon: Grammatically it is a possessive or subjective genitive (‘Christ’s mind’). In context (1 Cor 2:12–16) commentators usually take it to mean the Spirit-given understanding of Christ’s ways, not literally sharing Christ’s divine mind. The grammar supports ‘Christ’s mind’, but how far to push that is a matter of interpretation.

questions.q: Why does the series see Jesus’ baptism as one of the most important covenant transitions?
questions.a: John, a Levite, performed a cleansing like a priest’s ordination on Jesus, who was from Judah. That signalled the end of the Levitical priesthood and the start of the Melchizedek order. John’s willingness to decrease shows the old order handing over, and Israel crossing the Jordan behind the priests foreshadowed it.

questions.q: What does it mean that ‘the priest’s verdict stands’, and why does it make accusation so serious?
questions.a: Based on John 20:23, the sins believers forgive are forgiven and the sins they retain are retained. Since the priesthood’s task is to apply Christ’s finished work to creation, accusing others keeps them bound, while forgiveness frees them. So the series says holding creation in accusation kills it.

questions.q: How do the Red Sea and the Jordan differ in this teaching?
questions.a: At the Red Sea God did everything while the immature people stood still: grace brought them out of bondage. At the Jordan they had to be circumcised and step into the water before it parted. Entering the promise takes maturity, a deliberate act of will that aligns the soul with what has been won for us.

questions.q: Why did Joshua and Caleb not enter the promise alone, and what does that teach forerunners today?
questions.a: The promise had to be entered as one community, so the two faithful spies stayed in the wilderness with the next generation for forty years. Today’s ‘100-fold’ believers likewise cannot reign alone. They must show mercy as priests for those who do not yet see, instead of saying ‘thank God we’re not like them’.

questions.q: How does the sermon contrast Peter with Ananias and Sapphira and Stephen with his killers?
questions.a: The preacher says Peter retained the couple’s sins and they died, and he did not shine afterwards. Stephen forgave the men killing him, saw Jesus standing, had a face like an angel, and his mercy helped lead to Saul’s conversion. Human anger does not produce God’s righteousness.

questions.q: What are the three heavens, and how does each relate to a person?
questions.a: The first heaven is the seen, created realm, where the body is. The second is the unseen, created realm of angels, demons and the soul. The third is ‘heaven in God’, where the believer’s spirit is one with the Lord. Believers govern from the spirit, so they need not fight in the second heaven.

questions.q: According to this part, what is transfiguration and how does it happen?
questions.a: Transfiguration (metamorphoō) is divinity becoming visible in a human body, as with Jesus on the mountain. Believers experience it by renewing the mind: realising the carnal mind is dead, that they have Christ’s mind, and that they are beholding the Lord with unveiled face. Choosing to forgive, as Stephen did, is the practical doorway.

questions.q: Why does the preacher reject ‘glory to glory’ as a series of spiritual levels?
questions.a: He reads 2 Cor 3 as having only two glories: the glory of the law (death and condemnation), which shone on Moses’ face, and the glory of the Spirit and life. ‘From glory to glory’ describes moving out of the first into the second, being changed into the Lord’s image.

practice: Give up accusation, of individuals and of whole churches or regions. Choose to forgive instead.
Notice and turn away from ‘thank God I’m not like them’ thinking toward other denominations or groups.
Actively forgive and bless people who persecute or wrong you, as Stephen did.
Be a merciful forerunner: walk patiently with those who don’t yet see what you see, instead of going ahead alone.
Bring your soul into line with your spirit on purpose. Renew your mind by agreeing that you have the mind of Christ.
Govern from your identity in the spirit rather than being drawn into ‘second-heaven’ fights.
Value and care for your body as the means of dominion on earth.
Reflect the God you know: let people meet approval and life in you, not condemnation.

fair.claim: Jesus waited until thirty because that was the required age to be a rabbi.
fair.note: No known first-century rule set an age for becoming a rabbi. Luke says only that Jesus was ‘about thirty’. Thirty was the starting age for Levites serving at the tabernacle (Num 4:3). Charitably, the preacher may be thinking of the Levitical age, which would fit his priestly reading of the baptism.

fair.claim: Jews did not practise baptism, and John’s baptism was only a ‘Messiah test’ in which everyone in line thought they might be the Messiah.
fair.note: Second Temple Judaism practised ritual immersion (mikveh) and, by many accounts, immersion of converts. The Gospels describe John’s baptism as a baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins, with crowds confessing their sins, not as candidates for Messiah. The sign of the dove was given to John to identify the Messiah (John 1:33), which is the true part of the claim. Charitably: Jesus did not need repentance, so for Him the baptism served to reveal Him.

fair.claim: John had served in the priesthood six months and performed a Levitical priestly ordination on Jesus.
fair.note: John came from a priestly family, but the Gospels never show him serving in the temple. He lived in the wilderness (Luke 1:80). The Levitical ordination in Lev 8 involved washing, anointing and sacrifice by Moses at the tabernacle, which is quite different from John’s baptism in the Jordan. Hebrews says Jesus became a priest after Melchizedek’s order apart from Levitical descent, by divine oath, and does not link this to His baptism. Some interpreters see priestly overtones in the baptism, so the reading is possible typology, but it is not stated in Scripture.

fair.claim: Every human being, not only believers, is part of the Melchizedek priesthood and the ‘100-fold church’, and Hebrews 12 describes all humanity.
fair.note: 1 Pet 2:9 and Rev 1:5–6 address those who believe and have been redeemed. Heb 12:22–24 describes the ‘church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven’ and is addressed to believers, with a warning in the next verse not to refuse Him (12:25). Mainstream Christianity therefore limits the royal priesthood and the heavenly assembly to people in Christ. A charitable reading is that he means God’s intention for all people, or Christ’s representative work for all, which some Christian universalists and inclusivists hold.

fair.claim: Believers’ forgiveness or retention of sins decides others’ fate. Peter refused to forgive Ananias and Sapphira, and that is why their sins were retained and they died.
fair.note: John 20:23 is understood in different ways: as the church’s authority to declare forgiveness through the gospel (most Protestants), as sacramental absolution (Catholic and Orthodox), or as church discipline (compare Matt 18:18). Acts 5 does not say Peter withheld forgiveness. It says Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit and to God, and that God struck them. Peter did not tell Ananias ‘the Spirit is coming to kill you’. He announced judgment only to Sapphira. The text presents the deaths as God’s act, not Peter’s failure. Charitably, the preacher is rightly stressing that believers should prefer mercy (Jas 2:13).

fair.claim: Stephen was the ‘apostolic father’ or senior leader of the Jerusalem church, Saul actually said ‘kill him’, and Saul became Paul ‘in the very next chapter’.
fair.note: Stephen was one of the seven chosen to serve tables (Acts 6:5). The apostles, and later James, led the Jerusalem church. Acts says Saul approved of the killing and minded the witnesses’ garments (Acts 7:58; 8:1), not that he called for it. Stephen dies in Acts 7, and Saul’s conversion is in Acts 9, two chapters on. The point about Stephen’s forgiveness affecting Saul is a reasonable and widely shared reflection.

fair.claim: Stephen’s angel-like face appeared when he chose to forgive his persecutors.
fair.note: Acts 6:15 records the angel-like face at the start of his trial before the council, before his speech and before he was stoned and prayed for his killers (Acts 7:60). The tie between forgiveness and the shining face is the preacher’s link, not the order of events in the text.

fair.claim: God gave the land to Joshua alone (Josh 1:3), and it was then applied to the people through him.
fair.note: In Hebrew, Josh 1:3 says ‘I have given it to you’ with a plural ‘you’ (lakhem), echoing the promise to all Israel in Deut 11:24. So the verse is addressed to the people, not to Joshua alone. Joshua as a type of Christ (the names are the same in Greek: Iēsous) is an old and legitimate typology, but this verse does not show a victory given only to Joshua.

fair.claim: After the bad spies, God told Israel to go back and ‘try again’ with one mind, and Joshua and Caleb chose to return to the wilderness with the people for forty years.
fair.note: Numbers 14 presents the forty years as judgment on the unbelieving generation, which had to die in the wilderness. Joshua and Caleb were spared but shared the wandering by God’s decree, not by their own choice. The lesson about unity and patience is drawn by application, not stated in the text.

fair.claim: Joshua’s demanding ‘altar call’, including the ‘31 hostile empires full of giants’, happened just before entering the land, and then everyone possessed it at once.
fair.note: Joshua’s ‘you cannot serve the LORD’ exchange is in Josh 24, at the end of his life after the conquest, not before the crossing. The 31 were kings of city-states (Josh 12:24), not empires. Before the crossing the people pledged obedience to Joshua (Josh 1:16–18). The conquest took time, and some land was left unconquered (Josh 13:1).

fair.claim: At the Red Sea God said ‘be still and know that I am God’. At the Jordan He told them to plant gardens and make clothes.
fair.note: ‘Be still and know’ is Ps 46:10. At the Red Sea Moses said ‘stand still’ and that the LORD would fight for them (Exod 14:13–14). In the wilderness God supplied manna and their clothes did not wear out (Deut 8:4; 29:5). The manna stopped once they ate the land’s produce (Josh 5:12). The ‘plant a garden’ line is a loose dramatisation of that change.

fair.claim: Circumcision at Gilgal took away the sin of humanity, and the water stopping at the city of Adam means everything Adam produced became history.
fair.note: Josh 5:9 speaks of the ‘reproach of Egypt’, generally understood as the shame of slavery or of the uncircumcised wilderness generation, not humanity’s sin. The city Adam in Josh 3:16 is a place name. Reading it as a symbol of Adam’s legacy is an old devotional typology, not the plain sense. Both are best read as illustrative typology.

fair.claim: The human spirit of a believer is ‘uncreated’.
fair.note: Scripture describes God forming the human spirit (Zech 12:1) and the spirit returning to God who gave it (Eccl 12:7). Historic Christianity holds that only God is uncreated. Union with the Lord (1 Cor 6:17) and sharing in the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4) are usually understood as participation by grace, not as having an uncreated essence. Charitably, he may mean that the believer’s life comes from the uncreated Spirit of God.

fair.claim: Spiritual warfare is unnecessary, because believers simply govern and the devil cannot touch them.
fair.note: The NT tells believers to stand against the devil’s schemes and put on armour (Eph 6:10–18), to resist him (Jas 4:7; 1 Pet 5:8–9), and to tear down strongholds (2 Cor 10:3–5). 1 John 5:18 promises protection but does not cancel these commands. A charitable reading is that warfare should come from resting in Christ’s finished victory (Col 2:15) rather than anxious striving, which many teachers would agree with.

fair.claim: God cannot do what a human can do, and losing your body means losing your destiny, which is why physical immortality (not dying) matters so much.
fair.note: Scripture affirms God’s sovereignty and that He works through people, but not that He is unable to act on earth (Ps 115:3; Isa 46:10). The NT expects believers to die bodily unless Christ returns first (Heb 9:27; 1 Cor 15:51–52). It calls being away from the body and with the Lord ‘far better’ (Phil 1:21–23; 2 Cor 5:6–8), and places the believer’s bodily destiny in the future resurrection (1 Cor 15:42–54), not in avoiding death. The value placed on the body agrees with the biblical hope of resurrection.

fair.claim: Transfiguration, not the resurrection, was the moment Jesus ‘became divinity on earth’, and believers do not need to die to ‘be divine’.
fair.note: Historic Christology (Nicaea, Chalcedon) holds that Jesus was fully divine from the incarnation (John 1:1, 14; Col 2:9). The transfiguration revealed glory He already had (John 1:14; 2 Pet 1:16–18). It did not make Him divine. Saying humans ‘become divine’ goes beyond what Scripture says. Eastern Orthodox theosis speaks of sharing in God’s energies or life by grace (2 Pet 1:4), never of becoming God in essence. Charitably, he may mean the moment Jesus’ divinity became visible in His body.

fair.claim: ‘Transformed’ in Rom 12:2 is a bad translation, and metamorphoō means turning humanity into divinity.
fair.note: Metamorphoō means changing into another form. ‘Transformed’ is a standard and accurate rendering, and ‘transfigured’ is also possible. The preacher correctly counts its four NT uses (Matt 17:2; Mark 9:2; Rom 12:2; 2 Cor 3:18), though in 2 Cor 3 it is in verse 18, not verse 7. In Rom 12:2 the result of the change is discerning God’s will and living a sacrificial life (12:1–2), not becoming divine. The connection with Jesus’ transfiguration is a fair devotional observation.

fair.claim: The carnal mind has been removed entirely, and believers literally possess Christ’s own mind.
fair.note: Paul does say we have the mind of Christ (1 Cor 2:16), but in the same letter he calls the Corinthians fleshly (1 Cor 3:1–3). Elsewhere he urges believers to be renewed, to set their minds on the Spirit, and to take thoughts captive (Rom 8:5–6; Eph 4:22–24; 2 Cor 10:5), which assumes a continuing struggle. Mainstream teaching takes ‘mind of Christ’ as Spirit-given insight into God’s wisdom, together with ongoing renewal.

fair.claim: Doxa means ‘thoughts and opinions of’, so Moses’ face shone with the law’s disapproval and death, which is why people avoided him and why he veiled his face.
fair.note: In biblical Greek doxa mainly means glory, splendour or honour (Hebrew kabod). Exodus says Moses’ face shone because he had been speaking with the LORD (Exod 34:29), and Paul calls the old covenant ministry genuinely glorious, though fading and surpassed (2 Cor 3:7–11). Paul says Moses veiled himself so Israel would not gaze at the end of what was fading (3:13). That differs from saying the shine was condemnation. Paul’s point that the old covenant was a ‘ministry of condemnation’ is real, but the shine itself was God’s glory.

fair.claim: ‘From glory to glory’ means only two glories: from the law’s glory of death to the Spirit’s glory of life, not ongoing growth.
fair.note: Most commentators read apo doxēs eis doxan in 2 Cor 3:18 as a continuing, progressive change. The present tense ‘are being transformed’ supports this. Others take it as glory from the Lord producing glory in us. The preacher’s ‘two covenants’ reading is a minority interpretation. It fits the chapter’s old-versus-new contrast, but sits uneasily with the present continuous verb.

fair.claim: The folded head-cloth in John 20 is a prophetic picture of the head revealed and creation given victory.
fair.note: John records the detail mainly as evidence that the body was not stolen and as what led the beloved disciple to believe (John 20:8). Symbolic readings exist, but this one is devotional.

fair.claim: Isa 9:6 says ‘unto you’ a child is born, and the government being on His shoulders means it rests on His body, the church, not on His head.
fair.note: The text says ‘unto us’. ‘On His shoulder’ is a standard Hebrew image for carrying responsibility or authority (compare Isa 22:22). Reading it as head versus body is the preacher’s application. Ephesians does call Christ the head and the church His body (Eph 1:22–23), so the idea has a biblical anchor even if this verse does not teach it.

fair.claim: Jesus told the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector ‘twice’, and Paul wrote Hebrews 2.
fair.note: The parable appears once, in Luke 18:9–14 (the ‘twice’ may be emphasis). Hebrews is anonymous, and its authorship has been debated since the early church. Neither point changes the argument.

fair.claim: Paul was willing to have his name removed from the Book of Life for his fellow Jews.
fair.note: Rom 9:3 says Paul could wish himself ‘accursed (anathema), cut off from Christ’. The ‘blot me out of your book’ wording is Moses’ (Exod 32:32). The meaning is close, but the wording is a blend of the two.

fair.claim: A region’s disasters (California’s weather) may be linked to how much the church judges it.
fair.note: This is speculative, and Scripture warns against reading particular disasters as proof of particular guilt (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3). The underlying call, that believers should bless rather than curse the places they live, fits passages such as Jer 29:7 and Rom 12:14.

fair.claim: Three million Israelites left Egypt.
fair.note: This is a common estimate based on 600,000 men (Exod 12:37; Num 1:46). Some scholars read ’elef as ‘clan’ or ‘unit’ and arrive at far smaller numbers. It does not affect the point.
